title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (3 of 7)
hook: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar
carry: two, and the space between is love
tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (4 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vishishtadvaita: Ramanuja on the temple tower, and the world as God’s body. Your line: two, and the space between is love. Did you share something good you'd been keeping? Today, the question underneath all of this. Day two hundred ninety.

In Calcutta, the mystic Ramakrishna, whose student Vivekananda we met a few weeks ago, used to repeat a line from an old Bengali devotional song. People would ask him about merging into God, becoming one with the absolute, and he would answer, more or less: I don't want to become sugar. I want to taste sugar. It's a joke, and an argument. If you become the sugar, who's left to enjoy the sweetness?
screen: `CALCUTTA, RAMAKRISHNA.` → `I DON'T WANT TO BECOME SUGAR.` → `I WANT TO TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: The devotional schools make their case in that one line. Love, they say, needs two. A lover and a beloved. Someone to give and someone to receive. Someone to sing and someone to hear. Take away the difference, and you may have peace, or bliss, but you no longer have love in the way a mother loves a child, or a friend a friend. The Bhagavata Purana tells a story about this. Krishna has left the village where he grew up, and the cowherd women, the gopis, who loved him, are heartbroken. He sends his friend Uddhava, a learned man, to comfort them. And Uddhava comforts them with philosophy. Krishna is everywhere, he says; he's the self of all; you're never really apart from him. The gopis listen, and they answer, paraphrased: that's lovely. We want Krishna. Not the self of all. Him. His flute, his laugh, his face. Uddhava, humbled, says he would gladly be a bush or a creeper in their village, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. Other teachers explored the ground between. Nimbarka taught difference and non-difference at once. In Bengal, Chaitanya's followers called it inconceivable: one with God and different from God, both, beyond what the mind can hold. Now, fairly. Advaita teachers honor devotion too, as we heard with Bhaja Govindam, and some of them say love, fully ripened, dissolves into oneness. The devotional schools say love, fully ripened, stays two and grows forever. Hindus hold both, side by side. Nobody here has to pick.
screen: `LOVE NEEDS TWO.` · `THE GOPIS WANT KRISHNA, NOT A THEORY.` · `ONE AND DIFFERENT, BEYOND THOUGHT.` · `TWO VIEWS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and taste something, if you have it nearby: a sip of tea, a raisin, a square of chocolate. If not, remember one. Let it sit on the tongue. Notice the sweetness, and notice the one enjoying it. Two things: the taste, and the taster. Breathe in, and enjoy the difference. Breathe out, and let it be good. If you pray, you can let that enjoyment turn toward God, the way Ramakrishna meant it. The bell holds the time.
Gopis, the cowherd women who loved Krishna. Love needs a lover and a beloved; to taste sugar, you can't become it.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, eat one thing slowly enough to taste it, and let the tasting be a small thank-you. Day two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional traditions, teachers often explain that bhakti depends on the relationship between the devotee and God, and the gopis' love for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana is held up as its model.

fork.setup: you're one of the gopis. Uddhava tells you Krishna is the self of all, so you're never really apart from him. what do you say?
fork.reveal: they want Krishna himself, not an idea. Uddhava, the learned man, wished he could be a bush or a creeper in their village.

original.note: Sanskrit: achintya (inconceivable) + bheda-abheda (difference and non-difference): Chaitanya's school's view of God and soul.

trapdoor: what you thought: the highest goal in Hinduism is to merge into God.
what it means: that's one great view; devotional schools say the soul and God stay two, because love needs two.

what a scholar hears: the Uddhava–gopi dialogue is Bhagavata Purana 10.46–47 (incl. the Bhramara Gita); Nimbarka's school is dvaitadvaita, Chaitanya's acintya-bhedabheda; Ramakrishna's 'sugar' line echoes a song by Ramprasad Sen.

sources.ref: sayings of Ramakrishna as recorded by his disciples (the sugar image, echoing Ramprasad Sen)
Nimbarka (dvaitadvaita) and the Gaudiya school of Chaitanya (acintya-bhedabheda)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Uddhava's wish (Bhagavata 10.47.61) is to be a shrub, creeper or herb touched by the gopis' foot-dust, not 'a blade of grass'; corrected in the teach and fork. Removed 'nineteenth-century', 'for a thousand years', 'the whole argument' and 'many of them'; 'teachers after Ramanuja and Madhva' dropped because Nimbarka's date is disputed (tradition places him earlier). howItsDone no longer lists Shakta traditions for the gopi model or calls it 'highest'.

Ramakrishna's 'I want to taste sugar, not become sugar' is paraphrased; the English wording most people know comes from a 20th-century translation, so it isn't quoted. Confirm the Ramprasad attribution.
Uddhava's wish to be a blade of grass (or a shrub or herb) in Vrindavan is Bhagavata 10.47.61; confirm.
The balanced summary of Advaita vs devotional views follows the outline's 'never ranked'.
